# How this workbook works

Chapter 1 said you could put this book down for two weeks and pick it up
again. Here's what pays for that.

Every chapter after this one is built out of the same six parts, in the same
order, and each names the files it starts from. Coming back costs you a page of
reading, not an evening.

## The six parts

1. An opening question you can't answer yet, about real biology, with a real
   answer.
2. Concept, meaning the theory the next few pages need and none of the theory
   they don't.
3. Walkthrough, where I do the whole thing in front of you and print every
   output so you can hold your screen against the book.
4. Exercises, one or two, each stating what you'll produce and how long the
   work takes.
5. If it breaks, carrying the exact text of the errors that chapter produces.
6. Checkpoint, three to six things you can now do, in verbs somebody could
   watch.

This chapter has no exercises, because you haven't got a notebook yet. Chapter
4 hands you one.

## What a time estimate assumes

"About 25 minutes" on an exercise is an estimate, not a target. It assumes
you're typing the code rather than pasting it, and that the page you need loads
on the first try. It doesn't assume you already knew any of it.

Doubling that number is ordinary. I wrote every estimate already knowing the
answer, so they all lean short. If an exercise runs long, the estimate was
optimistic. Write down what it really cost you and use your own number next
time.

## The five labels

Five labels do the teaching here, each with a single job, and this page is the
only legend you'll get. Each one is set in italic and runs into the first line
of what it marks.

### Why this matters

A Why this matters note carries the biology that makes a technical thing worth
the trouble of learning.

::: {.why}
*BRCA1* occupies 126,033 bases of chromosome 17, and the transcript that gets
translated into protein is 7,088 bases. The rest is introns, cut out before the
protein is built. So "the length of *BRCA1*" isn't one number, and every length
in this book arrives with the name of the thing it measured.
:::

### Trap

A Trap marks something that runs cleanly and hands you a wrong answer.
Nothing turns red. These are the ones to read twice.

::: {.trap}
The human gene is `BRCA1`. The mouse one is `Brca1`, and two nomenclature
committees enforce that difference on purpose. Match a column of human symbols
against a table of mouse ones and you get no rows back. Nothing errors. You
lose an afternoon checking everything except the capital letters.
:::

### Check

A Check gives you a verification step and the exact output it should
produce.

::: {.check}
Turn to Chapter 5 and find all six parts in it. Only four carry a heading: the
opening question runs above the first one, and the checkpoint is the list at
the end. The exercises are numbered 5.1 and 5.2, and If it breaks holds four
errors. If you can't find the opening question, it's the pair of coordinates in
the first two paragraphs.
:::

### If it breaks

Each If it breaks note holds the exact text of an error, names who is speaking,
and gives the fix. An error stops you where you stand. A trap doesn't stop you
at all.

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="NameError: name 'seq' is not defined"}
Python is speaking here, and Python has no variable called `seq` at the moment
you asked for one. Usually the cell that creates `seq` is sitting above this
one, unrun. Run it, then run this one again.
:::
:::

### As of

An As of line carries a date. It appears wherever this book describes somebody
else's web page, because those pages get redesigned and nobody tells you.

::: {.asof}
Checked against the live NCBI Gene interface on 2 August 2026. The human
*BRCA1* record is Gene ID 672. NCBI moves the labels on that page every few
years. Gene ID 672 stays put.
:::

## Where the code and the answers live

Everything runnable in this book lives in one repository at
`github.com/rikhinkavuru/NoLabRequired`, together with the small data files
and a worked answer for every exercise. You'll open the first notebook from
there in Chapter 4.

That's the one full address the body of this book prints. Everywhere else you
get a bare domain like `ncbi.nlm.nih.gov`, because the domain is the part that
survives a redesign. Exact addresses live in the source index at the back, each
next to the date it was last checked.

## Type the code, don't copy it

This isn't about discipline.

Typing puts you in contact with syntax errors at a moment when nothing is at
stake. You'll miss a bracket, Python will refuse to run, you'll fix it in ten
seconds and forget it happened. That's the point. A reader who has never seen
`SyntaxError` in a safe moment meets it for the first time on a night when
something matters. They read it as a verdict on themselves rather than as a
missing bracket.

The counter-argument: it's faster to copy, and you're going to do it. I do it.
So the ask is narrower than "always type". Type it out the first time you meet
anything new, then copy freely after that.

Copying out of a PDF carries one mechanical hazard. A quote mark can arrive
curly where Python needs it straight, and Python rejects a curly quote with a
`SyntaxError`. Every code block in this book is checked for that before it
prints. What you copy from anywhere else isn't.

## When you're stuck

Every chapter has an If it breaks section near the end, holding the errors that
chapter really produces. This one produces none, because you haven't run
anything yet. So here's the general procedure. Work down it and stop at the
step that fixes things.

1. Read the last line of the error first. It names the error and what the
   machine couldn't do. The lines above are the route, not the problem.
2. Work out who's speaking. Python, the runtime your code runs on, a website
   and a silent network fail in four different ways, and Chapter 4 teaches the
   difference. Chapter 16 takes it apart error by error.
3. Look the message up in the error index at the back.
4. Restart and run every cell from the top. A notebook holds on to what earlier
   cells did, so the code on the page and the values in memory can disagree,
   with nothing on screen to say so.
5. Search for the exact message with your own filenames and variable names cut
   out of it. Keep the machine's words, drop yours.
6. Stop for the night. Write the last thing that worked into a text cell, and
   you'll pick it up faster tomorrow than you'll finish it tonight.

- Name the six parts of a chapter, in the order they appear
- Find all six in Chapter 5, and name the two that carry no heading
- Say what a Trap means, and how it differs from an If it breaks note
- Say what an exercise's time estimate assumes about how you're working
- Name the first line to read when an error appears
:::
